hypotheses.note: not used: only Convex ℝ (U ∪ V) is assumed (Lean ≥ paper); prop1_supports_printed carries them
affineSpan ℝ U, affineSpan ℝ V

findings: Prop. 1 (l.1169–1175) is imprecise: its first sentence (one support contains the other) is true without exception (prop1_supports), but the « façon plus précise » (l.1172–1174) fails when U = V = {p}: no point is aligned with two distinct points of a singleton (not_prop1_precisPrinted). This is the only exception (prop1_precis: the dichotomy holds or U = V = {p}). The exception consists of two NON-DISJOINT sets, which § 5's title (« Sur les convexes, réunions de deux convexes disjoints », l.1150) rules out: for disjoint U, V the precise form holds (prop1_precis_of_disjoint).

The printed proof (l.1177–1181) claims « le segment demi-ouvert ]a, b] soit contenu dans U »; the endpoint b need not be in U (U = [0,1[, V = {1}, a = 0); the open segment )a, b( ⊆ U suffices for the conclusion, and the case b = a (forcing V = {a}) is not treated. Neither the convexity of U nor of V is used.
questions: « aligné avec deux points distincts de V » read as: ∃ b ≠ c in V with a on the line bc (a may be b or c). The exception U = V = {p} fails under every reading.

Is the disjointness of § 5's title a standing hypothesis of Prop. 1? Prop. 1 itself does not say « disjoints ». Reading taken: no, so the row stays partial (imprecise); under the title's reading the precise form is proved in full (prop1_precis_of_disjoint) and the row could be marked — the author's decision.

labels.label: bzprop:c3s5p6_contact_convexe

hypotheses.note: the true form adds Convex ℝ (U ∪ V), the setting of § 5 (title l.1150) and of Prop. 7 (F = contact set of V and W − V, W convex)

findings: Prop. 6 (l.1244) is FALSE as printed, under both readings of « alignés » in Déf. 2: in ℝ³, U = {z = 0, y < 0} ∪ {(0,0,0)} and V = {y = 0, z > 0} ∪ {(2,0,0)} are disjoint convex sets whose contact set contains (0,0,0) (A ∈ U, C = (0,0,1)) and (2,0,0) (A ∈ V, B = (2,−1,0)) but not their midpoint (1,0,0): B − P must lie in the plane z = 0 and C − P in the plane y = 0, so collinearity forces both on the x-axis, where U and V have only (0,0,0) and (2,0,0) (not_convex_ensembleContact, not_convex_ensembleContactEntre). The counterexample uses degenerate witnesses (B = A for (0,0,0), C = A for (2,0,0)), which the printed convention )A, A( = {A} of Déf. 2 explicitly allows; under a reading demanding B ≠ A ≠ C, these two points would not be contact points of these sets.

The printed proof (l.1248–1256) is right except for alignment: B″ = (1−λ)B + λB′, C″ = (1−λ)C + λC′ satisfy )B″, A″( ⊆ U and )A″, C″( ⊆ V, but B″, A″, C″ need not be aligned. It proves that the contact set WITHOUT the alignment condition is convex, for any two convex sets (convex_contactSansAlignement).

Prop. 6 is true when U ∪ V is convex (convex_ensembleContact_of_convex_union, and for the « entre » reading): then every contact point lies in U ∪ V (using U ∩ V = ∅), and a point of U ∪ V in the alignment-free contact set is a contact point (take B = A or C = A). This covers § 5's use in Prop. 7 (l.1265), where F is the contact set of V and W − V, whose union W is convex.

kb_proposals: Chapter3/ProprieteI: « V fermé » in a bare vector space is best stated as FermeLineaire (every line meets V in a closed parameter set) plus fermeLineaire_of_isClosed for any topology with continuous lines — one theorem covers « fermé » for every topology in which lines are continuous.

Chapter3/ProprieteI: Benzécri's contact set F (Déf. 2) is NOT convex in general (ℝ³ counterexample); it is convex when U ∪ V is convex (§ 5's setting). Later § 5 targets (Prop. 7, Thms 1, 1′) should use convex_ensembleContact_of_convex_union.
Collinear {B, A, C} → coordinates: collinear_iff_of_mem (p₀ := A) gives B = r₁•v + A, C = r₂•v + A (vadd_eq_add); then split on r₁ = 0, r₂ = 0, sign of r₁r₂ — no need for B ≠ A.

Points of an open segment in coordinates: hB ⟨1/2, 1/2, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩ then simp only [Prod.smul_mk, Prod.mk_add_mk, smul_eq_mul] turns membership into linear facts in products r*v_i, which linarith treats as atoms.
